PART 1: NARRATION READY
Let's talk about what your REND1 transformer is telling us — because this field has a clear story, and the numbers make it easy to read. You're running a 2,500 kVA transformer at Foster Farms Livingston. Right now, that field is operating at 79.8% power factor. What that means in plain language is that roughly 20% of the electrical capacity you're pulling from the utility every day is doing no productive work. It's circulating as reactive current — spinning through your motors and transformer windings — generating heat and cost without producing a single watt of output. The reactive load on this transformer peaks at 1,194 kVAR. Your transformer is carrying a thermal burden of 880,313 BTUs per hour as a direct result. And you're spending approximately $221,000 a year just on cooling costs to manage the heat that a correctable inefficiency is generating. When you add up the reactive energy waste, the thermal losses, and the cooling overhead, you arrive at a total annual waste figure of approximately $658,000 per year on this transformer alone. Monthly, that's roughly $34,400 in documented energy loss. The voltage picture adds another layer. Your field is running persistently above nominal — 476.7 volts average on a 480-volt system — and you're seeing recurring voltage dip events throughout May, with the worst dropping to 454.9 volts. That's a 25-volt swing below nominal on a system where your motors, drives, and controls are expecting a stable supply. That bidirectional voltage cycling accelerates equipment aging. MPTS correction targeting 99.5% power factor would require three H490 units for full correction. At planning-level estimates, that's roughly $600,000 installed. Against $658,000 in annual waste, the projected payback is approximately 10 to 11 months. That is a measurable, engineering-grounded correction opportunity — and this field is ready for it. ---

PART 2: EXECUTIVE SHORT
Here's the executive summary on REND1. You have a 2,500 kVA transformer running at 79.8% power factor, carrying 1,194 kVAR peak reactive demand, and generating 880,313 BTUs per hour of thermal burden. Total annual waste — reactive losses, thermal burden, and cooling overhead combined — is approximately $658,000. The correction requires three H490 MPTS units, at a planning-level installed investment of approximately $600,000. The projected payback is roughly 10 to 11 months. Beyond the financial recovery, correction reduces transformer thermal stress, recovers 128.4 kilowatts of cooling load, and improves voltage stability for the motors and drives on this circuit — all of which extend equipment life and improve operational reliability. The field is untuned, the waste is active, and the correction opportunity is clearly defined. That's where REND1 stands today. --- Pricing note: these figures are planning-level estimates, not final quotes. Final installed pricing depends on engineering scope, labor, and site conditions. For planning, estimated installed investment is roughly $510,000 to $690,000.

PART 3: ENGINEERING DETAILED
Let's go deeper on REND1, because this transformer's field has several layers of stress happening simultaneously — and understanding all of them is what separates a good correction project from a complete one. Start with the power factor. At 79.8%, REND1 is operating with a significant reactive burden. Power factor is essentially the ratio of real work being done to total electrical capacity being drawn. A 79.8% power factor means that for every 1,000 kVA you're pulling from the utility, only 798 kW is doing productive work. The remaining 202 kVA equivalent is reactive current — it's not working, but it is flowing through every conductor, every connection, every winding in the system. That reactive current has a thermal cost. Your transformer's winding resistance doesn't care whether current is reactive or active — it heats up either way. The result is a thermal burden of 880,313 BTUs per hour being dissipated by this transformer and its associated distribution circuit. That heat has to go somewhere, and it costs you approximately $25.32 per hour and 128.4 kilowatts of continuous cooling load to manage it. Over a year, that cooling overhead alone is approximately $221,823. The reactive demand peaks at 1,194.2 kVAR during production peaks. That's the number that drives the MPTS sizing calculation. Using the Unity sizing rule — divide 1,194.2 kVAR by 400 and round up — you arrive at 3 H490 units. Each H490 delivers 400 kVAR of correction, so three units give you 1,200 kVAR of correction capacity, which fully covers your peak reactive demand and brings your power factor to approximately 99.5%. At planning-level estimates, three H490 units installed represents roughly $600,000, subject to engineering scope and site conditions. Now let's look at the voltage picture, because it's not just about reactive correction. The V view shows a field running above nominal — 476.7 volts average on a 480-volt nominal system, with peaks touching 489.3 volts. That above-nominal operating point is a chronic insulation stress condition. Every hour of operation above nominal is accelerating dielectric aging in motor windings, transformer insulation, and cable insulation systems. Layered on top of that, you have nine or more annotated voltage dip events across May, with the most severe reaching 454.9 volts — a 25-volt drop below nominal, or about 5.2%. These are transient but they're recurring, and they cluster in the final week of May with increasing severity. The combination of chronic above-nominal bias and recurring below-nominal dip events creates a bidirectional voltage stress envelope that shortens equipment life over time. This is what moderate device health risk looks like in practice. The two confirmed outage events in early May — visible as gold streak events in the BT and B chart views, estimated at four to seven combined minutes — are brief, but in a food processing and rendering environment, even minutes of unplanned interruption carry real operational and food safety implications. Bringing this all together: the total annual waste figure for REND1 is approximately $658,109 — reactive losses, thermal burden, and cooling overhead combined. MPTS correction at three H490 units targets the majority of that waste, with a projected payback of approximately 10 to 11 months at planning-level estimates. Alongside the financial recovery, you're reducing transformer thermal stress, recovering 128 kilowatts of cooling capacity, extending motor and winding life, and building in reactive margin that makes the field more resilient to the voltage disturbances we're already seeing. That's electromagnetic stewardship — and that's the Unity standard. ---

**REND1 — Voltage Health Analysis | May 2026**

The voltage story on REND1 has two layers, and both of them matter. The first layer is the high-side bias: your field is running with an average voltage of 476.7 volts against a 480V nominal. That sounds close, but the maximum touches 489.3 volts — and sustained operation above nominal accelerates insulation aging on motor windings, drives, and transformer windings. This is a chronic, continuous stress condition, not a transient event.

The second layer is the recurring dip profile. The V view shows annotated triangular drop events distributed across the full month — nine or more distinct excursion events — with voltage dips reaching as low as 454.9 volts in the final week of May. A 454.9-volt reading is approximately 25 volts below nominal, or about a 5.2% downward excursion. In a 480V industrial system serving motors, VFDs, and control equipment, that kind of repeated cycling through a wide voltage band — from above 480V down to sub-460V and back — creates bidirectional stress that accelerates component fatigue over time.

The dip events are not random. They cluster in the middle two weeks of May and again in the final week, with the final-week cluster containing the most severe readings: 455.5V and 454.9V. This suggests a developing or worsening condition in the last operating week of the dataset — worth watching for recurrence.

The minimum recorded voltage of 9.5 volts confirms at least one full power interruption occurred during the month. Combined with the visual identification of two distinct top-to-bottom gold streak events in the BT and B chart views — at approximately the May 8th and May 11th markers — this field experienced two outage events with a combined estimated duration of roughly four to seven minutes. These were brief interruptions, but in a food processing and rendering environment, even a few minutes of unplanned downtime carries operational and product safety implications.

Device health risk assessment: **Moderate.** The bidirectional voltage stress profile, combined with recurring dip events below nominal and confirmed outage activity, places connected equipment — particularly motors, drives, and any sensitive control systems — in an elevated fatigue risk category.

This field shows the classic signature of a well-utilized industrial transformer that has never received reactive compensation. Let's read the stress indicators together.

Transformer loading is at 72.8% average capacity, with peaks reaching 1,773.7 kVA against a 2,500 kVA nameplate — that's 70.9% peak loading. In absolute terms, this is within the transformer's operating range, but the thermal burden of 880,313 BTU per hour tells you the transformer is running hot. A significant fraction of that thermal load is reactive-origin: the reactive current is circulating through every winding, every conductor, and every connection point in the system, generating I²R losses across the entire circuit. Reduce the reactive current and you directly reduce the thermal burden.

The cooling overhead is quantified in the BT header: approximately $25.32 per hour and 128.4 kW of cooling load — costing an estimated $221,823 per year just to manage the heat generated by a correctable inefficiency. That's not a small number. That's a dedicated cooling infrastructure cost that exists largely because the field is uncompensated.

The production rhythm in the BT and B views is clear — four to five production week blocks across May, with the field spending an estimated 55 to 60% of its operating time above the 1,399 kVA supply target line during active production shifts. This means the transformer is regularly operating above its daily planned supply capacity during peak production hours, which compounds the thermal and reactive stress during the hours when operational reliability matters most.

The two confirmed outage events in early May — brief but confirmed by both the gold streak visual indicators and the 9.5V minimum reading — are a reminder that this field is not operating with margin to spare. An uncompensated, thermally stressed transformer field has less resilience to voltage disturbances and switching events. Reactive correction directly improves that margin.

Sizing the correction: applying the Unity sizing rule — kVAR MAX divided by 400, rounded up — gives us 1,194.2 ÷ 400 = 2.985, which rounds up to **3 H490 units**. At planning-level estimates, three H490 units represent an installed investment of approximately $600,000, subject to final engineering scope, site conditions, and any required switchgear or integration work. This is a planning-level range, not a binding quote.

Against an annual total waste cost of approximately $658,109 — reactive losses, thermal burden, and cooling overhead combined — a three-unit H490 correction targeting near-unity power factor projects a recovery of the majority of that annual waste. Using the Total Wasted figure of $658,109 as the pre-correction baseline, the projected payback window falls in the range of approximately 10 to 11 months at planning-level estimates, assuming full field correction is achieved and maintained.

Beyond the financial recovery, the operational benefits are concrete: transformer thermal burden drops significantly, reducing winding stress and extending equipment service life. Cooling load decreases, recovering an estimated 128.4 kW of cooling overhead. Amperage peaks are reduced, improving conductor life and reducing the probability of thermally-driven breaker trips. And voltage stability at the transformer secondary improves, directly benefiting the motor and drive loads that are currently cycling through the bidirectional voltage stress profile we observed in the V view.

REND1.recommended_engineering_attention_areas:
**REND1 — Engineering Attention Areas | May 2026**

The following areas warrant engineering review prior to or concurrent with MPTS correction planning for REND1.

**Reactive compensation sizing:** Three H490 units are required to address the 1,194.2 kVAR MAX demand. Engineering should confirm reactive demand profile across shift patterns and seasonal load cycles — May represents one month's behavior, and sizing should account for peak reactive demand across the full operating year.

**Voltage operating point:** The field runs persistently above nominal at 476.7V average with peaks to 489.3V. Engineering should review utility tap settings and transformer LTC or tap changer position to determine if the high-side operating point can be optimized. Reducing the chronic above-nominal operating voltage will extend insulation life across all connected equipment.

**Recurrent dip events:** Nine or more annotated voltage dip events, with the final week showing the most severe excursions to 454.9V, suggest a developing source of disturbance — potentially load-switching transients, transformer inrush events, or upstream utility disturbances. Root cause investigation is warranted before and after MPTS installation to establish a pre- versus post-correction comparison baseline.

**Outage root cause:** Two confirmed brief outage events occurred in early May, estimated at four to seven combined minutes. In a food processing and rendering environment, even brief outages carry product safety and process continuity implications. Engineering should verify whether these were utility-side events or facility-side switching and assess whether MPTS correction and improved power factor margin would reduce their probability or severity.

**Harmonic monitoring:** Current iTHD peaks at 10.7%. While not the primary concern, ongoing monitoring is recommended, particularly if additional VFDs or nonlinear loads are added to this transformer's distribution circuit. Harmonic filters may become appropriate if the iTHD profile worsens post-correction.
